strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP efficiency problem: selecting a teacher without expensive distillation searches. The GPT-2 and Pythia experiments provide useful evidence that larger teachers can produce worse compressed students.

MiniMA shows practical gains across knowledge, reasoning, coding, and English/Chinese benchmarks. In Table 2, it outperforms the reported compute-comparable ShearedLLaMA baseline on all six tasks, including MMLU (28.51 versus 26.15) and GSM8K (8.11 versus 5.26). The LLaMA3.1 experiment further demonstrates the recipe's usefulness.

The pruning and distillation objectives are straightforward, and symmetric student architectures support deployment with standard libraries. Code/model links, data-mixture statistics, detailed LLaMA training settings, and evaluation protocols facilitate reuse.
weaknesses: The central 2.5× law is insufficiently established. Since S approximately equals (1−p)T, selecting 60% sparsity already implies T approximately equals 2.5S; the substantive question is whether that sparsity is consistently optimal. Figure 3 contains irregularly spaced student sizes, but the procedure for deriving Figure 4's optimal-teacher pairs, including any interpolation, is unclear. The reported R²=0.9957 lacks uncertainty estimates and held-out prediction errors, and does not establish a unique optimum rather than a broad near-optimal range.

Teacher size is entangled with pruning severity, inherited weights, and potentially student architecture because each student is constructed from its teacher. This limits attribution to capacity gap itself. Furthermore, Table 2 tests only one larger student size, approximately 3B: 7B outperforming 13B and 70B supports the capacity-gap phenomenon but does not precisely locate the optimum or validate linear scaling across larger students. Table 4 keeps teacher/student sizes fixed, so similar performance under alternative methods cannot establish that their optimal ratios remain unchanged. Controlled student configurations and additional teacher sweeps are needed.

The claimed compute–performance frontier uses incomplete accounting. Appendix H assigns MiniMA approximately 4.0×10^9 TFLOPs for distillation but omits the 126B-token teacher-adaptation stage described in Appendix A. Under Equation 7, adapting the 7B teacher adds approximately 5.3×10^9 TFLOPs, before pruning costs. Shared or amortized costs should be identified explicitly. Rumor-based assumptions about Mistral training tokens and GPT-4 parameters further weaken the frontier comparison.

Reproducibility is weakest for the pilot experiments underpinning the main claim. The reduced training budget is described only as 'fewer tokens,' pilot-specific optimization settings are missing, and exact measurements used to construct the fitted relation are not supplied. The resulting architectures and adaptation treatment of the 13B/70B teacher experiments also require clarification. These gaps, together with the unresolved optimality claim, prevent a positive Findings recommendation at present.

The instruction-following evaluation provides limited support for broad superiority claims. GPT-4 version and response-order controls are unspecified, while the human assessment lacks annotator counts, judgment counts, and uncertainty estimates. Spearman correlation 0.54 is incorrectly interpreted as 54% consistency. Appendix J also acknowledges possible contamination behind instruction-tuning benchmark gains, limiting their evidential value.

strengths: Addresses a practical NLP efficiency problem: selecting a teacher without repeatedly running expensive distillation experiments. Predicting suitable teacher size is a useful research direction.

The GPT2 and Pythia experiments cover multiple pruning levels and two evaluation metrics, while the LLaMA experiments extend the investigation to larger models. These results support the observation that larger teachers can produce worse students.

Table 2 demonstrates practical benefits of the MiniMA recipe: it outperforms the compute-matched ShearedLLaMA baseline on all six reported benchmarks, including MMLU (28.51 versus 26.15) and DROP (22.50 versus 20.03).

weaknesses: The central claim of a unique, setting-independent teacher size near 2.5 times the student size is insufficiently established. Figures 3–4 use sparse teacher/pruning grids without clearly explaining how optimal teachers are selected or interpolated at matched student sizes. Selecting pairs near 60% pruning already constrains their size ratio near 2.5; the resulting high R² does not independently validate the predictive claim. Controlled validation at held-out student sizes and uncertainty estimates around the selected optima are needed.

The extrapolation and ablations provide limited tests of the proposed law. The compute–performance frontier uses incomplete and uncertain accounting. Table 10 reports approximately 4.0e21 FLOPs for MiniMA distillation but omits the additional teacher adaptation in Appendix A. Using the paper’s own formula, adapting a 7B teacher on 126B tokens adds approximately 5.3e21 FLOPs. Competitor estimates, particularly Phi’s synthetic-data costs, also depend on speculative GPT4 architecture and insufficiently justified token accounting. The claimed frontier requires consistent cost boundaries and sensitivity analysis.

The manuscript does not specify the precise reduced-token budget or a complete pilot optimization configuration, and provides no uncertainty estimates or numerical results sufficient to reconstruct the optimum-selection and fitting procedure. The instruction-following evaluation provides weaker support than the broad capability claims suggest. The human assessment omits annotator and judgment counts and uncertainty intervals; Spearman correlation of 0.54 is incorrectly interpreted as 54% consistency. Appendix J also acknowledges unresolved contamination in the instruction-tuning benchmark gains. These limitations should constrain the conclusions drawn from the secondary evaluations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: selecting an effective teacher without expensive distillation searches. A reliable relationship between teacher and student sizes would be useful for NLP model compression.

The GPT2 and Pythia experiments cover multiple teacher sizes, pruning ratios, two evaluation metrics, and a reduced-data setting. They provide useful evidence that larger teachers need not produce better pruned students under the tested procedure.

MiniMA shows promising practical results. Table 2 reports improvements across all six benchmarks over the evaluated pruning baselines, including the compute-comparable ShearedLLaMA variant. Experiments with LLaMA3.1 and bilingual instruction tuning broaden the application evidence.

The manuscript provides explicit pruning and distillation objectives, substantial large-model training details, data-mixture statistics, and links to code and checkpoints. Producing symmetric architectures compatible with standard libraries is a sensible implementation choice.
weaknesses: The central 2.5× scaling law is not established sufficiently for a positive Findings recommendation. Figure 4 does not adequately explain how optimal teachers are identified at matched student sizes from Figure 3's sparse grids. Because student size is approximately (1−sparsity) times teacher size, selecting points near 60% sparsity already induces the reported relationship. The high R² therefore needs independent support through explicit optimum selection, uncertainty estimates, and prediction on held-out configurations; it does not establish uniqueness or generality by itself.

Teacher size is confounded with the student's inherited architecture, initialization, and pruning severity. A student pruned from a larger teacher can perform worse because its initialization or architectural proportions are less favorable, without establishing a general limitation of distillation across capacity gaps. Comparisons using a common student architecture and initialization, together with corresponding no-distillation controls, would distinguish these explanations. Figure 9 supplies training losses rather than downstream results for its no-distillation control.

The extrapolation and ablations do not validate the claimed invariance. Table 2 primarily establishes that 7B is better than 13B and 70B for the tested approximately 3B student; one student size cannot validate the proposed scaling relationship. Likewise, Table 4 changes pruning and distillation methods at a single teacher–student configuration, so it cannot establish that their optimal ratios remain unchanged. Multiple student sizes and searches around predicted optima are needed, or the claims should be narrowed to a procedure-specific heuristic.

The compute–performance frontier uses incomplete accounting. Table 10 reports approximately 4.0×10^9 TFLOPs for MiniMA, but Appendix A describes an additional 126B-token adaptation of its 7B teacher. Equation 7 assigns approximately 5.3×10^9 TFLOPs to that adaptation alone, before pruning costs. Even treating original teacher pretraining as a sunk cost, this expense needs inclusion or explicit amortization. Rumor-based assumptions for competing models further weaken the frontier claim.

Reproducibility is weakest for the experiments supporting the law. The manuscript does not specify the reduced token budget, clearly document pilot optimization settings, provide exact student configurations and numerical optimum-selection data, or report variation across runs. It is also unclear whether the larger LLaMA2 teachers receive adaptation equivalent to the 7B teacher. These omissions affect interpretation of the central comparisons.

The instruction-following evaluation warrants more cautious conclusions. Judge versions, response-order controls, human comparison counts, and uncertainty estimates are not adequately reported. Appendix L incorrectly interprets a Spearman correlation of 0.54 as 54% consistency. The practical results are encouraging, but these evaluation limitations and the central validation and accounting issues require revision before acceptance.

The GPT2 and Pythia experiments cover multiple model sizes and pruning ratios, with evaluation on WikiText2 and LAMBADA. They provide useful evidence that increasing teacher size can worsen student performance under the studied procedure.

The larger-model experiments demonstrate a promising compression recipe. In Table 2, the 7B-to-3B MiniMA outperforms the reported 252B-token ShearedLLaMA baseline across all six benchmarks, and generally exceeds students derived from larger LLaMA2 teachers.

weaknesses: The central capacity-gap law is insufficiently established for a positive Findings recommendation. Each student is pruned and initialized from its respective teacher, so changing teacher size also changes inherited weights, student architecture, and pruning severity. The observed optimum could therefore reflect properties of this compression procedure. Controlled comparisons using a common student architecture and initialization, or substantially narrower claims, are needed.

The derivation of Figure 4 is underspecified: the manuscript does not explain how optimal teachers at fixed student sizes are selected from the discrete teacher–sparsity grid, including any interpolation. Since approximately 60% sparsity already implies S ≈ 0.4T, the high regression R² cannot independently establish that this ratio is optimal. The extrapolation and ablations do not establish the claimed generality. MiniMA shows practical promise. Table 2 reports improvements over the compute-adjusted ShearedLLaMA baseline on all six benchmarks, including MMLU (28.51 versus 26.15) and GSM8K (8.11 versus 5.26). The evaluation covers English, Chinese, reasoning, and coding.

Explicit pruning and distillation equations, data-mixture statistics, detailed large-model training settings, and repository/model links support reuse. The symmetric architecture also provides a practical implementation benefit.
weaknesses: The central claim of a reliable, uniquely optimal teacher scale is insufficiently established. Sections 3.4–3.5 do not explain how optimal teachers are selected at matched student sizes from Figure 3's sparse teacher/sparsity grid, including any interpolation or reconciliation between evaluation metrics. Since S approximately equals (1−p)T by construction, high R² among selected pairs near 60% sparsity does not independently establish that this sparsity is optimal. The fitting needs transparent selection procedures, uncertainty estimates, and held-out predictive validation.

Teacher size is confounded with student initialization, architecture, and pruning severity: each student inherits parameters from its respective teacher. Larger teachers undergo more severe pruning to reach the same student size. Consequently, performance degradation cannot be attributed specifically to distillation capacity rather than pruning damage and recovery difficulty. Common-student controls or matched pruning-and-recovery experiments are needed; otherwise, the claim should be restricted to the evaluated procedure.

The extrapolation and ablations do not establish the claimed generality. Table 2 compares 7B, 13B, and 70B teachers for one approximately 3B student size. Finding 7B best among these candidates supports that selection but does not validate linear scaling across larger student sizes. Likewise, Table 4 compares methods at one size pair; similar performance there does not demonstrate that their optimal teacher/student ratios coincide.

The compute-performance frontier requires revised accounting. Table 10 reports approximately 4.0 × 10⁹ TFLOPs for MiniMA's distillation but excludes the 126B-token teacher adaptation described in Appendix A. Under Equation 7, that stage adds approximately 5.3 × 10⁹ TFLOPs. A comparison conditional on an already-adapted teacher can be useful, but its scope and amortization must be explicit. Speculative baseline costs based on rumored GPT4 architecture and training budgets also require sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility is weakest for the central scaling study. The manuscript does not specify the reduced-token budget, pilot optimization settings, or sufficient numerical data to reconstruct the optimum-selection analysis, and it reports no run variability. It is also unclear whether the 13B/70B teachers and compression baselines receive the same Chinese adaptation as the 7B teacher. These omissions affect interpretation of the main comparisons.

The instruction-following evidence needs stronger validation. Appendix J acknowledges unresolved potential benchmark contamination. Appendix L omits judgment and annotator counts and incorrectly interprets Spearman correlation 0.54 as 54% consistency. The coding solution presented favorably in Table 13 also incorrectly returns the first array when the second is empty. These secondary problems, together with the unresolved identification and reproducibility of the primary law, warrant resubmission next cycle rather than a Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: selecting an effective teacher for language-model compression without an expensive search. Investigating a predictable teacher–student size relationship is a worthwhile empirical objective.

The experiments cover GPT-2 and Pythia model families, variation in distillation data quantity, and larger LLaMA-based models. Table 2 reports consistent MiniMA improvements over the listed compression baselines, including longer-trained ShearedLLaMA: MMLU increases from 26.15 to 28.51 and GSM8K from 5.26 to 8.11.

The pruning and distillation objectives are clearly specified. Large-model training settings, data-mixture statistics, and benchmark protocols are documented, and links to code and model checkpoints support potential reuse.
weaknesses: The central law is insufficiently established. Figure 3 connects results at generally different student sizes, but the procedure for matching or interpolating these results into the fixed-student optima of Figure 4 is unspecified. Since S approximately equals (1−p)T, selecting sparsities near 60% already produces T approximately equal to 2.5S. The reported R² summarizes these selected points; it does not independently establish their optimality, uniqueness, or predictive accuracy. Explicit comparisons at fixed student sizes, uncertainty estimates, and held-out predictions are needed.

The larger-model experiments provide limited validation of the scaling relation. Table 2 shows that a 7B teacher outperforms the tested 13B and 70B teachers for a single 3B student size, with the winner at the boundary of the tested teacher sizes. This supports a capacity-gap observation but does not identify the predicted optimum or validate the slope across student sizes. Likewise, Table 4 evaluates alternative methods at one teacher–student configuration, so comparable performance there does not establish that their optimal ratios remain unchanged.

Teacher size is entangled with the compression procedure: students inherit different weights and pruning damage from their respective teachers, and their architectures can differ. The evidence therefore supports a relationship conditional on this pipeline. The claims of broad applicability require stronger controls or narrower framing. It is also unclear whether the larger teachers and compression baselines receive the same vocabulary adaptation and additional data exposure as the adapted 7B teacher.

The compute–performance claim needs corrected accounting. Appendix H reports approximately 4.0×10^9 TFLOPs for MiniMA, but Appendix A describes an additional 126B-token adaptation of its 7B teacher. Under the paper’s own formula, that adds approximately 5.3×10^9 TFLOPs before pruning and distillation. Meanwhile, some competing models receive speculative synthetic-data production costs. The Pareto comparison needs a consistent accounting boundary and sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility is weakest precisely where the law is derived: the manuscript does not specify the reduced-token budget, sufficient pilot-training hyperparameters, or the numerical observations and selection procedure underlying the fitted optima. Repeated-run variability is also unreported. The secondary human evaluation omits judgment and annotator counts, and interpreting Spearman correlation 0.54 as 54% agreement is incorrect. These reporting gaps, together with the central validation issues, warrant revision before a Findings recommendation.
